Bellman Policy Optimization

Zhuoqing Song Affiliation: Apodex US, Inc. Affiliation: Princeton University    Haotian Xu Affiliation: Apodex US, Inc.    Xikun Zhang Affiliation: Apodex US, Inc.    Lidong Bing Affiliation: Apodex US, Inc.
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). We introduce Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free method derived from Policy Mirror Descent (PMD). For autoregressive generation with terminal rewards, BPO uses the Bellman equations to reformulate PMD as a trajectory-level objective. The reformulation avoids estimating state values at intermediate states. We prove that it has the same unique optimal solution as the original PMD objective. We derive the practical BPO loss by approximating this objective. Its mismatch-correction weight is a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of BPO.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. In RLVR, models are trained using outcome-level rewards assigned to generated responses by task-specific verifiers. Recent work has shown that choices in policy optimization can have a substantial impact on both reasoning performance and training stability [4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11].

Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and its variants are widely used in RLVR [1, 4, 12, 7, 13, 14, 8, 15]. GRPO samples multiple responses for each prompt and computes advantages by normalizing their rewards within the group. Under outcome supervision, all tokens in a response share the same advantage. GRPO uses these advantages in a PPO-style clipped surrogate objective with token-level importance-sampling ratios [16]. This formulation and its variants avoid training a value model and support large-scale reasoning-model training [2, 3, 5, 13, 17, 18, 19].

We start from Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) [20, 21]. PMD updates the policy using action values and a divergence penalty. However, directly applying this update to language generation requires value estimates at intermediate states. A common approach is to train a separate value model, which increases memory and computational costs [1]. Learned value estimates can also be inaccurate on reasoning tasks [22]. We seek a reformulation of PMD that recovers the same policy update without training a value model.

We introduce Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free policy optimization method derived from PMD. Our derivation builds on prior work that reparameterizes rewards and values using policy likelihood ratios [23, 24, 25, 11]. For autoregressive generation with terminal rewards, the Bellman equations express each token advantage as a difference between value functions at consecutive states. These differences telescope along a response, leaving only the terminal reward and the initial value. We combine this identity with the PMD optimality condition to derive a trajectory-level objective. The initial value is the expected reward for a prompt and can be estimated from sampled responses. The reformulation therefore avoids estimating values or advantages at intermediate states. We prove that this objective and the original PMD objective have the same unique optimal solution on states reachable under the rollout policy.

We then derive the practical BPO loss through a sequence of approximations. We estimate the initial value using the mean reward of responses sampled for each prompt. We approximate the gradient of the trajectory-level objective and replace the full KL divergence with a binary approximation [8]. The resulting gradient includes a mismatch-correction weight determined by the rollout and current token probabilities. We apply additive smoothing to this weight for numerical stability. In the practical BPO loss, this weight replaces the importance-sampling ratio used in GRPO.

We evaluate BPO on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k. We compare against GRPO-ClipHigher [1, 4], GSPO [7], CISPO [13], and DPPO [8] under identical experimental settings. As shown in Figure 1, BPO achieves a peak average accuracy of 50.5%50.5\% across AIME 2024–2026 [26]. The gains over these four baselines are 11.011.0, 7.07.0, 3.13.1, and 4.14.1 percentage points, respectively.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We derive a critic-free, trajectory-level reformulation of PMD for autoregressive generation with terminal rewards, avoiding value or advantage estimation at intermediate states. We prove that this reformulation and the original PMD objective have the same unique optimal solution on states reachable under the rollout policy.

  • •

    We derive the practical BPO loss from this reformulation through group-based estimation and gradient approximations. The loss replaces GRPO’s importance-sampling ratio with a mismatch-correction weight given by a smoothed ratio of complementary token probabilities.

  • •

    We evaluate BPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. BPO achieves a peak average accuracy of 50.5%50.5\% across AIME 2024–2026, outperforming GRPO-ClipHigher, GSPO, CISPO, and DPPO by 3.13.1–11.011.0 percentage points.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notation

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the vocabulary. Let xx denote a prompt and let y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) denote a response. Both xx and yy are token sequences over 𝒱\mathcal{V}. In response yy, yty_{t} is the tt-th token and the length TT may vary across responses. We also use |y||y| to denote its length.

For 1≤t≤u≤T1\leq t\leq u\leq T, let yt:u=(yt,…,yu)y_{t:u}=(y_{t},\ldots,y_{u}) denote the subsequence of yy from positions tt through uu. We write y<t=y1:t−1y_{<t}=y_{1:t-1}, y≤t=y1:ty_{\leq t}=y_{1:t}, and y≥t=yt:Ty_{\geq t}=y_{t:T}.

For any token sequences z1,…,zkz_{1},\ldots,z_{k}, (z1,…,zk)(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}) denotes their concatenation. For instance, (x,y<t)(x,y_{<t}) denotes the prompt xx followed by the response subsequence y<ty_{<t}. For a function whose argument is a token sequence, we write f⁡(z1,…,zk)f(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}) as shorthand for f⁡((,,,,,))f((z_{1},\ldots,z_{k})) whenever no ambiguity arises.

2.2 RLVR as an Episodic MDP

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large language models (LLMs) can be formulated as a finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Process (MDP).

Let DD denote a prompt set and let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote a prompt distribution on DD. We assume 𝒟\mathcal{D} is uniform on DD for simplicity. The analysis extends directly to more general prompt distributions.

States and transitions.

For a prompt x∈Dx\in D, the initial state s1s_{1} is defined as the sequence xx itself. At step t>1t>1, the state sts_{t} concatenates the prompt xx and the generated prefix y<ty_{<t}: st=(x,y<t).s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}). The transition is deterministic: appending token yty_{t} to st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) yields the next state st+1=(x,y≤t)s_{t+1}=(x,y_{\leq t}).

Policies and completion distributions.

Let Δ(𝒱)={p:𝒱→[0,1]|∑v∈𝒱p(v)=1}\Delta(\mathcal{V})=\left\{p:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow[0,1]|\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p(v)=1\right\} denote the set of probability distributions on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. A stochastic policy is a mapping π:𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒱)\pi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{V}). In particular, π(⋅|x,y<t)∈Δ(𝒱)\pi(\cdot|x,y_{<t})\in\Delta(\mathcal{V}) denotes the next-token distribution at position tt. The policy space is denoted by Π=Δ​(𝒱)𝒮\Pi=\Delta(\mathcal{V})^{\mathcal{S}}. For any policy π\pi, let Ππ⊆Π\Pi_{\pi}\subseteq\Pi denote the set of policies that are absolutely continuous with respect to π\pi.

For any policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, we use ℙπ(⋅|st)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot|s_{t}) to denote the completion distribution induced by π\pi, i.e., ℙπ​(y≥t|st)=∏u=t|y|π⁡(yu|su)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(y_{\geq t}|s_{t})=\prod_{u=t}^{|y|}\pi(y_{u}|s_{u}), where y≥t=yt:|y|y_{\geq t}=y_{t:|y|} as mentioned in Section 2.1.

The action at step tt is the tt-th token yty_{t} in the generated response, and is sampled from the policy π(⋅|x,y<t)\pi(\cdot|x,y_{<t}). In practice, π\pi is parameterized by an autoregressive LLM. The response y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) terminates when the EOS token is generated or the response length limit TmaxT_{\max} is reached.

Rewards and objective.

A deterministic verifier RR assigns the terminal reward. Without loss of generality, we assume |R⁡(x,y)|≤1|R(x,y)|\leq 1 for any prompt-response pair (x,y)(x,y).

The policy objective is

𝒥(π)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼ℙπ(⋅|x)[R(x,y)].{}\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot|x)}\left[R(x,y)\right].\end{split} (1)

2.3 Group-Relative Policy Optimization

In practical RLVR, responses are generated by a rollout policy μ\mu, while policy optimization is performed on the current policy π\pi. Policy updates between rollout generation and training steps, together with numerical discrepancies between the rollout and training engines, can cause the two policies to differ [27, 28, 8, 29, 30]. Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [1] is a critic-free, PPO-style policy optimization method [16]. For each prompt x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, GRPO independently samples a group of GG responses {yi}i=1G\left\{y^{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{G} from ℙμ(⋅|x)\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x). Let Ri=R⁡(x,yi)R_{i}=R(x,y^{i}) denote the reward of response yiy^{i}. GRPO assigns each response the group-normalized advantage

A^i=Ri−mean​({Rj}j=1G)std​({Rj}j=1G).{}\begin{split}\hat{A}^{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\texttt{mean}\big(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)}{\texttt{std}\big(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)}.\end{split} (2)

GRPO applies PPO-style clipping to the token-level importance ratio. For the tt-th token in response yiy^{i}, its per-token loss is defined as

ℒi,tGRPO​(π)=−min⁡{rti​A^i,clip⁡(rti,1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)​A^i},{}\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\pi)=-\min\left\{r_{t}^{i}\hat{A}^{i},\;\mathrm{clip}\left(r_{t}^{i},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right)\hat{A}^{i}\right\},\end{split} (3)

where rtir_{t}^{i} is the token-level importance ratio defined as

rti=π⁡(yti|sti)μ⁡(yti|sti).{}\begin{split}r_{t}^{i}=\frac{\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}{\mu(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}.\end{split} (4)

The following per-token loss has the same gradient as (3) and is therefore equivalent for gradient-based training:

ℒ~i,tGRPO​(π)=−A^i​Mti​sg​(rti)​log⁡π⁡(yti|sti),{}\begin{split}\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\pi)=-\hat{A}^{i}M_{t}^{i}\texttt{sg}\left(r_{t}^{i}\right)\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}),\end{split} (5)

where the clipping mask MtiM_{t}^{i} is defined as

Mti={0,A^i>0​ and ​rti>1+ϵhigh,0,A^i<0​ and ​rti<1−ϵlow,1,otherwise.{}\begin{split}M_{t}^{i}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0,&\hat{A}^{i}>0\text{ and }r_{t}^{i}>1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}},\\ 0,&\hat{A}^{i}<0\text{ and }r_{t}^{i}<1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},\\ 1,&\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\end{split} (6)

2.4 Bellman Equations with Terminal Rewards

We next introduce value functions and Bellman equations [31] for the terminal-reward setting described in Section 2. For a fixed policy π\pi and state st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}), define the value function as the expected reward under policy π\pi given state sts_{t}, i.e.,

Vπ(st)=𝔼z∼ℙπ(⋅|st)[R(x,(y<t,z))],{}\begin{split}V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot|s_{t})}\left[R(x,(y_{<t},z))\right],\end{split} (7)

where the expectation is taken over all completions under policy π\pi given state st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}). The initial value Vπ​(s1)=Vπ​(x)V^{\pi}(s_{1})=V^{\pi}(x) is therefore the expected reward for prompt xx under policy π\pi.

Since intermediate rewards are zero, for a non-terminal state sts_{t}, the action-value function is defined as

Qπ(st,yt)=𝔼s′∼ℙ(⋅|st,yt)[Vπ(s′)]=Vπ(st+1),{}\begin{split}Q^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}(\cdot|s_{t},y_{t})}\left[V^{\pi}(s^{\prime})\right]=V^{\pi}(s_{t+1}),\end{split} (8)

where st+1=(st,yt)s_{t+1}=(s_{t},y_{t}) and the second equality follows from the deterministic transition described in Section 2.

For a non-terminal state sts_{t}, the advantage function is defined as

Aπ​(st,yt)=Qπ​(st,yt)−Vπ​(st).{}\begin{split}A^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})=Q^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})-V^{\pi}(s_{t}).\end{split} (9)

The advantage function Aπ​(st,yt)A^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t}) measures how favorable the current action yty_{t} is at state sts_{t} relative to the expected action value under policy π(⋅|st)\pi(\cdot|s_{t}). It follows from (7) and (9) that

∑yt∈𝒱π⁡(yt|st)​Aπ​(st,yt)=0.{}\begin{split}\sum_{y_{t}\in\mathcal{V}}\pi(y_{t}|s_{t})A^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})=0.\end{split} (10)

For any non-terminal state sts_{t}, the Bellman equation is

Vπ(st)=∑yt′∈𝒱π(yt′|st)Qπ(st,yt′)=∑s′=(st,yt′):yt′∈𝒱π(yt′|st)Vπ(s′).\begin{split}V^{\pi}(s_{t})=\sum_{y_{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\pi(y_{t}^{\prime}|s_{t})Q^{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t}^{\prime})=\sum_{s^{\prime}=(s_{t},y_{t}^{\prime}):y_{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\pi(y_{t}^{\prime}|s_{t})V^{\pi}(s^{\prime}).\end{split}

For a complete response yy, the terminal state is s|y|+1=(x,y)s_{|y|+1}=(x,y). The terminal condition is

Vπ​(s|y|+1)=R⁡(x,y).\begin{split}V^{\pi}(s_{|y|+1})=R(x,y).\end{split}

2.5 Policy Mirror Descent

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the state space, and let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the vocabulary as in Section 2. Given a real-valued function f:𝒮×𝒱→ℝf:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) [32, 20, 21, 33] solves the following optimization problem for each state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}:

maxπ(⋅|s)∈Δ(𝒱)𝔼y∼π(⋅|s)[f(s,y)]−1ηDKL(π(⋅|s)∥μ(⋅|s)),{}\begin{split}\max_{\pi(\cdot|s)\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\quad\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}\left[f(s,y)\right]-\frac{1}{\eta}{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s))},\end{split} (11)

where μ\mu is the behavior policy (rollout policy) and η>0\eta>0 is the step size.

The optimization problem (11) has the unique solution

πμ,f+​(y|s)=μ⁡(y|s)​exp⁡(η​f​(s,y))Zμ,f​(s),{}\begin{split}\pi^{+}_{\mu,f}(y|s)=\frac{\mu(y|s)\exp\left(\eta f(s,y)\right)}{Z_{\mu,f}(s)},\end{split} (12)

where the partition function is

Zμ,f(s)=𝔼y′∼μ(⋅|s)exp(ηf(s,y′)).\begin{split}Z_{\mu,f}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim\mu(\cdot|s)}\exp\left(\eta f(s,y^{\prime})\right).\end{split}

2.6 Binary KL Divergence

Let π,μ∈Π\pi,\mu\in\Pi be two policies on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. For a fixed state ss, their KL divergence is

DKL(π(⋅|s)∥μ(⋅|s))=∑y∈𝒱π(y|s)logπ⁡(y|s)μ⁡(y|s).\begin{split}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s))=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\pi(y|s)\log\frac{\pi(y|s)}{\mu(y|s)}.\end{split}

Computing the full KL divergence requires logits for the entire vocabulary and can be costly.

The binary KL divergence introduced in [8] approximates the full KL divergence. For a given action y∈𝒱y\in\mathcal{V}, it partitions the action space into {y}\left\{y\right\} and its complement 𝒱∖{y}\mathcal{V}\setminus\left\{y\right\}. This induces the following Bernoulli distributions:

πbiny(⋅|s)=(π(y|s),1−π(y|s)),μbiny(⋅|s)=(μ(y|s),1−μ(y|s)).\begin{split}\pi^{\mathrm{bin}}_{y}(\cdot|s)=\left(\pi(y|s),1-\pi(y|s)\right),\quad\mu^{\mathrm{bin}}_{y}(\cdot|s)=\left(\mu(y|s),1-\mu(y|s)\right).\end{split}

We define the binary KL divergence associated with action yy as

DbinKL(π(⋅|s)∥μ(⋅|s);y)=DKL(πbiny(⋅|s)∥μbiny(⋅|s))=π⁡(y|s)​log​π⁡(y|s)μ⁡(y|s)+(1−π⁡(y|s))​log​1−π⁡(y|s)1−μ⁡(y|s).{}\begin{split}&\quad D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\pi(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s);y\right)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\pi^{\mathrm{bin}}_{y}(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu^{\mathrm{bin}}_{y}(\cdot|s)\right)\\ &=\pi(y|s)\log\frac{\pi(y|s)}{\mu(y|s)}+\left(1-\pi(y|s)\right)\log\frac{1-\pi(y|s)}{1-\mu(y|s)}.\end{split} (13)

As shown in [8], binary KL divergence provides a lower bound for KL divergence, i.e.,

0≤DbinKL(π(⋅|s)∥μ(⋅|s);y)≤DKL(π(⋅|s)∥μ(⋅|s)),∀y∈𝒱.\begin{split}0\leq D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\pi(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s);y\right)\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\pi(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s)\right),\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}.\end{split}

3 Bellman Policy Optimization

We first define the BPO loss and then derive it from PMD.

BPO Loss Definition.

For each prompt x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, we independently sample a group of GG responses {yi}i=1G\left\{y^{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{G}. For the tt-th token of response yiy^{i}, the BPO loss is

ℒBPO​(π)=−A^i​Mti​min⁡{sg​(ωti),C}​log⁡π⁡(yti|x,y<ti),{}\begin{split}\mathcal{L}^{\text{BPO}}(\pi)=-\hat{A}^{i}M^{i}_{t}\min\left\{\texttt{sg}\left(\omega^{i}_{t}\right),C\right\}\log\pi(y^{i}_{t}|x,y^{i}_{<t}),\end{split} (14)

where A^i\hat{A}^{i} is the advantage of response yiy^{i} in the group {yi}i=1G\left\{y^{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{G} defined in (2) and the terms ωti\omega^{i}_{t}, CC, and MtiM^{i}_{t} are defined below:

  • •

    ωti\omega^{i}_{t} is the mismatch-correction weight for the tt-th token in response yiy^{i}, defined as

    ωti=1+ϵ−μ⁡(yti|x,y<ti)1+ϵ−π⁡(yti|x,y<ti),{}\begin{split}\omega^{i}_{t}=\frac{1+\epsilon-\mu(y^{i}_{t}|x,y^{i}_{<t})}{1+\epsilon-\pi(y^{i}_{t}|x,y^{i}_{<t})},\end{split} (15)
  • •

    The constant CC caps ωti\omega^{i}_{t} to stabilize training. The mask MtiM_{t}^{i} follows the GRPO clipping rule in (6), with the weight ωti\omega_{t}^{i} replacing the importance-sampling ratio:

    Mti={0,A^i>0​ and ​ωti>1+ϵhigh0,A^i<0​ and ​ωti<1−ϵlow1,otherwise.\begin{split}M^{i}_{t}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0,&\hat{A}^{i}>0\text{ and }\omega^{i}_{t}>1+\epsilon_{\text{high}}\\ 0,&\hat{A}^{i}<0\text{ and }\omega^{i}_{t}<1-\epsilon_{\text{low}}\\ 1,&\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\end{split}

The BPO per-token loss retains the GRPO form in (5) and replaces the importance-sampling ratio rtir_{t}^{i} with the truncated mismatch-correction weight min⁡{sg​(ωti),C}\min\left\{\texttt{sg}\left(\omega_{t}^{i}\right),C\right\}.

Derivation of the BPO Objective.

We derive the BPO objective (14) in three steps:

  • •

    Step 1 (Starting Point, (16)): we instantiate PMD with f⁡(s,y)=Aμ​(s,y)f(s,y)=A^{\mu}(s,y), where Aμ​(s,y)A^{\mu}(s,y) is the advantage function introduced in Section 2.4.

  • •

    Step 2 (Critic-free PMD, Section 3.1): we derive a critic-free objective with the same optimal solution as advantage-based PMD. This avoids estimating Aμ​(s,y)A^{\mu}(s,y) at individual states.

  • •

    Step 3 (Practical Approximation, Section 3.2): we approximate the critic-free PMD objective from Step 2 to obtain the BPO objective (14).

Starting Point: Advantage-Based PMD.

We first instantiate the general PMD objective in (11) with the rollout-policy advantage Aμ​(s,y)A^{\mu}(s,y) of the terminal-reward MDP in Section 2.4, i.e., f⁡(s,y)=Aμ​(s,y).f(s,y)=A^{\mu}(s,y). Classical PMD is commonly formulated using the action-value function Qμ​(st,yt)Q^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t}) [32, 20, 21, 33]. Using AμA^{\mu} gives the same update because Qμ​(st,yt)=Aμ​(st,yt)+Vμ​(st),Q^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})=A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})+V^{\mu}(s_{t}), and the term Vμ​(st)V^{\mu}(s_{t}) does not depend on the action yty_{t}.

Advantage-based PMD solves the following problem for each state st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}):

maxπ(⋅|st)∈Δ(𝒱)𝔼yt∼π(⋅|st)[Aμ(st,yt)]−1ηDKL(π(⋅|st)∥μ(⋅|st)).{}\begin{split}\max_{\pi(\cdot|s_{t})\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\quad\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t})}\left[A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})\right]-\frac{1}{\eta}{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\mu(\cdot|s_{t}))}.\end{split} (16)

As discussed in Section 2.5, the optimization problem (16) has the unique solution π+\pi^{+}, given at each state st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) by

π+​(yt|st)=μ⁡(yt|st)​exp⁡(η​Aμ​(st,yt))Zμ​(st),{}\begin{split}\pi^{+}(y_{t}|s_{t})=\frac{\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})\exp\left(\eta A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})\right)}{Z_{\mu}(s_{t})},\end{split} (17)

where the partition function is

Zμ(st)=𝔼y′t∼μ(⋅|st)exp(ηAμ(st,y′t)).\begin{split}Z_{\mu}(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}_{t}\sim\mu(\cdot|s_{t})}\exp\left(\eta A^{\mu}(s_{t},y^{\prime}_{t})\right).\end{split}

Here, we use π+\pi^{+} and ZμZ_{\mu} as abbreviations for πμ,Aμ+\pi^{+}_{\mu,A^{\mu}} and Zμ,AμZ_{\mu,A^{\mu}}.

3.1 Critic-Free Reformulation of Policy Mirror Descent

Directly implementing the update (16) requires estimating Aμ​(st,yt)A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t}) at every visited intermediate state. This typically requires a learned critic or costly conditional rollouts. We derive the critic-free reformulation in (18) by expressing rewards and values through policy likelihood ratios and the Bellman equations. This follows prior work on direct alignment [23, 24, 25, 11].

Critic-Free Reformulation of PMD.

Let μ\mu denote the rollout policy. We assign each prompt x∈Dx\in D a fixed positive weight ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). We will specify this weight in Section 3.2 to obtain the practical BPO loss. We consider the following critic-free objective:

minπ∈Πμℒ(π)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼ℙμ(⋅|x)[ϕ(x)⋅δ​(x,y,π,μ)22​η],{}\begin{split}\min_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mu}}\mathcal{L}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x)}\left[\phi(x)\cdot\frac{\delta(x,y;\pi,\mu)^{2}}{2\eta}\right],\end{split} (18)

where the trajectory-level residual δ⁡(x,y,π,μ)\delta(x,y;\pi,\mu) is defined as

δ(x,y;π,μ)=η(R(x,y)−Vμ(x))−∑t=1|y|(logπ⁡(yt|st)μ⁡(yt|st)+DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π(⋅|st))).{}\begin{split}\delta(x,y;\pi,\mu)=\eta\big(R(x,y)-V^{\mu}(x)\big)-\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\Big(\log\frac{\pi(y_{t}|s_{t})}{\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})}+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}))\Big).\end{split} (19)

The reformulation (18) does not depend on state-value functions at intermediate states. Instead, it only requires the terminal reward R⁡(x,y)R(x,y) and the initial value function Vμ​(x)V^{\mu}(x). The terminal reward R⁡(x,y)R(x,y) is directly provided by the verifier, while Vμ(x)=𝔼y∼ℙμ(⋅|x)[R(x,y)]V^{\mu}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x)}\left[R(x,y)\right] is the expected reward for prompt xx under the rollout policy μ\mu. We can estimate this expectation from rollout data.

Equivalence to PMD.

Theorem 1 shows that the critic-free objective (18) and PMD (16) have the same unique optimal solution. This equivalence holds for any positive weighting function ϕ\phi. We specify ϕ\phi in Section 3.2 when deriving the practical BPO loss (14).

Theorem 1.

Let the policy π+\pi^{+} in (17) denote the optimal solution of the PMD problem (16). Let ϕ:D→ℝ+\phi:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} be any positive weight function on the prompt set DD. For any prompt x∈Dx\in D, we solve the optimization problem (18). Then, this optimization problem admits a unique optimal solution π^+\hat{\pi}^{+} which equals π+\pi^{+}. Here, uniqueness and equivalence are in the sense that any policy π^+∈Πμ\hat{\pi}^{+}\in\Pi_{\mu} that solves (18) induces the same completion distribution as π+\pi^{+} for every prompt x∈Dx\in D, i.e., ℙπ^+(⋅|x)=ℙπ+(⋅|x)\mathbb{P}_{\hat{\pi}^{+}}(\cdot|x)=\mathbb{P}_{\pi^{+}}(\cdot|x).

We now derive objective (18) and outline the proof of Theorem 1.

Derivation and Proof of Sufficiency.

We first explain how we derive the critic-free objective (18) from the original advantage-based PMD (16) and show that the PMD solution π+\pi^{+} minimizes the reformulated objective (18).

∙\bullet Step 1: We rewrite (17) as the PMD optimality condition and eliminate the state-dependent partition function Zμ​(st)Z_{\mu}(s_{t}). For any prompt xx, response yy, and step tt with 1≤t≤|y|1\leq t\leq|y|, we can rewrite (17) as

log⁡π+​(yt|st)−log⁡μ⁡(yt|st)−η​Aμ​(st,yt)+log⁡Zμ​(st)=0.{}\begin{split}\log\pi^{+}(y_{t}|s_{t})-\log\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})-\eta A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})+\log Z_{\mu}(s_{t})=0.\end{split} (20)

Taking the expectation over yt∼μ(⋅|st)y_{t}\sim\mu(\cdot|s_{t}) and using (10) gives

logZμ(st)=DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π+(⋅|st))+η∑yt∈𝒱μ(yt|st)Aμ(st,yt)=DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π+(⋅|st)).{}\begin{split}\log Z_{\mu}(s_{t})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi^{+}(\cdot|s_{t}))+\eta\sum_{y_{t}\in\mathcal{V}}\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi^{+}(\cdot|s_{t})).\end{split} (21)

Then, substituting (21) into (20) yields

logπ+(yt|st)−logμ(yt|st)−ηAμ(st,yt)+DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π+(⋅|st))=0.{}\begin{split}\log\pi^{+}(y_{t}|s_{t})-\log\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})-\eta A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi^{+}(\cdot|s_{t}))=0.\end{split} (22)

∙\bullet Step 2: We next express the cumulative token-level advantages in terms of the terminal reward. By the Bellman equation, substituting (8) into (9) gives

Aμ​(st,yt)=Vμ​(st+1)−Vμ​(st).\begin{split}A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})=V^{\mu}(s_{t+1})-V^{\mu}(s_{t}).\end{split}

Summing over the trajectory gives

∑t=1|y|Aμ​(st,yt)=Vμ​(s|y|+1)−Vμ​(s1)=R⁡(x,y)−Vμ​(x).{}\begin{split}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})=V^{\mu}(s_{|y|+1})-V^{\mu}(s_{1})=R(x,y)-V^{\mu}(x).\end{split} (23)

∙\bullet Step 3: For any prompt-response pair (x,y)(x,y), summing (22) over the trajectory and using (23) gives

∑t=1|y|(logπ+(yt|st)−logμ(yt|st)+DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π+(⋅|st)))=η(R(x,y)−Vμ(x)),\begin{split}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\left(\log\pi^{+}(y_{t}|s_{t})-\log\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi^{+}(\cdot|s_{t}))\right)=\eta\left(R(x,y)-V^{\mu}(x)\right),\end{split}

i.e.,

δ⁡(x,y,π+,μ)=0.{}\begin{split}\delta(x,y;\pi^{+},\mu)=0.\end{split} (24)

Minimizing the expected squared residual under the rollout distribution gives (18).

Proof Sketch of Necessity.

It remains to show that every optimal solution of (18) coincides with π+\pi^{+} on all states reachable under μ\mu. Define the token-level residual

dπ(st,yt)=ηAμ(st,yt)−(logπ(yt|st)−logμ(yt|st)+DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π(⋅|st))).\begin{split}d_{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})=\eta A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})-\Big(\log\pi(y_{t}|s_{t})-\log\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}))\Big).\end{split}

For any feasible policy π\pi for which the above quantities are finite, its conditional expectation under the rollout policy is zero:

𝔼yt∼μ(⋅|st)[dπ(st,yt)]=η∑yt∈𝒱μ(yt|st)Aμ(st,yt)−∑yt∈𝒱μ(yt|st)logπ⁡(yt|st)μ⁡(yt|st)−DKL(μ(⋅|st)∥π(⋅|st))=0.\begin{split}\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\mu(\cdot|s_{t})}\left[d_{\pi}(s_{t},y_{t})\right]=\eta\sum_{y_{t}\in\mathcal{V}}\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})A^{\mu}(s_{t},y_{t})-\sum_{y_{t}\in\mathcal{V}}\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})\log\frac{\pi(y_{t}|s_{t})}{\mu(y_{t}|s_{t})}-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}))=0.\end{split}

Therefore, the cumulative token-level residuals form a martingale under the rollout policy μ\mu. For any optimal solution of (18), the terminal value of this martingale equals the trajectory-level residual and is zero almost surely. Since the response length is bounded by TmaxT_{\max}, the martingale property then implies that every partial sum is zero almost surely. Thus, each token-level residual vanishes. The complete proof is provided in Appendix A.1.

3.2 Practical Approximation

We obtain the practical BPO loss (14) by approximating the critic-free objective (18). We linearize the squared-residual objective and estimate the initial value and prompt-dependent scaling factor from grouped rollouts. We then approximate the full reverse KL divergence using binary KL divergence and apply smoothing, masking, and clipping.

For response yiy^{i}, define the response-level loss ℒi​(π)=ϕ⁡(x)​δ​(x,yi,π,μ)2/(2​η)\mathcal{L}_{i}(\pi)=\phi(x)\delta(x,y^{i};\pi,\mu)^{2}/(2\eta). Its gradient can be decomposed into token-level contributions ∇ℒi​(π)=∑t=1|yi|∇ℒi,t​(π).\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}(\pi)=\sum_{t=1}^{|y^{i}|}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}(\pi). Throughout this section, ∇\nabla denotes the gradient with respect to the parameters of π\pi with μ\mu fixed.

∙\bullet Step 1: linearized approximation. We linearize the squared-residual loss with respect to the residual δ\delta, around its value at π=μ\pi=\mu. Since δ⁡(x,yi,μ,μ)=η⁡(R⁡(x,yi)−Vμ​(x))\delta(x,y^{i};\mu,\mu)=\eta\left(R(x,y^{i})-V^{\mu}(x)\right), this replaces the residual factor δ⁡(x,yi,π,μ)/η\delta(x,y^{i};\pi,\mu)/\eta in the gradient by R⁡(x,yi)−Vμ​(x)R(x,y^{i})-V^{\mu}(x). For response yiy^{i} and the corresponding state sti=(x,y<ti)s_{t}^{i}=(x,y_{<t}^{i}), the per-token gradient contribution is approximated by

∇ℒi,t​(π)=−ϕ(x)δ⁡(x,yi,π,μ)η∇(logπ(yti|sti)+DKL(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti)))≈−ϕ(x)(R(x,yi)−Vμ(x))∇(logπ(yti|sti)+DKL(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti))).{}\begin{split}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}(\pi)&=-\phi(x)\frac{\delta(x,y^{i};\pi,\mu)}{\eta}\nabla\Big(\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i}))\Big)\\ &\approx-\phi(x)\Big(R(x,y^{i})-V^{\mu}(x)\Big)\nabla\Big(\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i}))\Big).\end{split} (25)

∙\bullet Step 2: group-based estimation and normalization. The initial value function Vμ(x)=𝔼y∼ℙμ(⋅|x)[R(x,y)]V^{\mu}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x)}\left[R(x,y)\right] has the unbiased estimator mean​({R⁡(x,yj)}j=1G)\texttt{mean}\big(\{R(x,y^{j})\}_{j=1}^{G}\big). We further choose ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) as the inverse reward standard deviation, i.e., ϕ⁡(x)=1Vary∼ℙμ(⋅|x)(R(x,y))\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{Var}_{y\sim\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x)}(R(x,y))}}. We replace it by its empirical counterpart ϕ⁡(x)≈1std​({R⁡(x,yi)}i=1G)\phi(x)\approx\frac{1}{\texttt{std}\big(\{R(x,y^{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}\big)}. With these substitutions, (25) becomes

∇ℒi,t(π)≈−A^i∇(logπ(yti|sti)+DKL(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti))).{}\begin{split}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}(\pi)\approx-\hat{A}^{i}\nabla\Big(\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i}))\Big).\end{split} (26)

∙\bullet Step 3: binary KL approximation and additive smoothing. Computing the full reverse KL divergence in (26) can be costly. We therefore replace the full KL divergence DKL(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})) in (26) with the binary KL divergence DKLbin(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti);yti)D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i});y_{t}^{i}\right) as defined in Section 2.6. As proved in Appendix A.2, the following identity holds

∇(logπ(yti|sti)+DbinKL(μ(⋅|sti)∥π(⋅|sti);yti))=1−μ⁡(yti|sti)1−π⁡(yti|sti)∇logπ(yti|sti).{}\begin{split}\nabla\Big(\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})+D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s_{t}^{i})\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s_{t}^{i});y_{t}^{i}\right)\Big)={\frac{1-\mu(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}{1-\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}}\nabla\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}).\end{split} (27)

Substituting (27) into (26) gives

∇ℒi,t(π)≈−A^i1−μ⁡(yti|sti)1−π⁡(yti|sti)∇logπ(yti|sti).{}\begin{split}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}(\pi)\approx-\hat{A}^{i}{\frac{1-\mu(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}{1-\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}}\nabla\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}).\end{split} (28)

The multiplier 1−μ⁡(yti|sti)1−π⁡(yti|sti)\frac{1-\mu(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})}{1-\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i})} in (28) can become large when π⁡(yti|sti)\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}) approaches one. We use the additively smoothed mismatch-correction weight ωti\omega_{t}^{i} defined in (15) for numerical stability. The resulting per-token gradient is

∇ℒi,t(π)≈−A^iωti∇logπ(yti|sti).{}\begin{split}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}(\pi)\approx-\hat{A}^{i}\omega_{t}^{i}\nabla\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}).\end{split} (29)

∙\bullet Step 4: masking and clipping. The preceding steps yield the approximate per-token gradient direction −A^iωti∇logπ(yti|sti).-\hat{A}^{i}\omega_{t}^{i}\nabla\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}).

We apply the GRPO-style clipping mask MtiM_{t}^{i} and cap ωti\omega_{t}^{i} at CC. The resulting per-token BPO loss gradient is

∇ℒi,tBPO(π)=−A^iMtimin{ωti,C}∇logπ(yti|sti).\begin{split}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{BPO}}(\pi)=-\hat{A}^{i}M_{t}^{i}\min\left\{{\omega_{t}^{i}},C\right\}\nabla\log\pi(y_{t}^{i}|s_{t}^{i}).\end{split}

This gives the BPO loss (14).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate BPO on mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base [3]. All methods are trained on the English subset of DAPO-Math-17k [4]. We compare BPO with GRPO-ClipHigher [1, 4], GSPO [7], CISPO [13], and DPPO [8]. We conduct controlled comparisons by varying only the policy loss and keeping all other experimental settings identical.

Each rollout batch contains 256 prompts with 16 responses per prompt. The resulting 4096 responses are split into 8 minibatches of 512 responses. One training step consists of one rollout batch followed by its eight minibatch updates. We train each method for 400 training steps, corresponding to 3200 optimizer updates. The maximum response length is 16384 tokens. All methods use rollout-router replay (R3) [34]. BPO uses ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1 and C=3.0C=3.0. Ablations on these hyperparameters are presented in Appendix C. More details are given in Appendix B.

We evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26 [26]. We estimate Pass@1 using Avg@32: we sample 32 responses per question, average their correctness, and then average over questions. The average accuracy is the arithmetic mean of the three benchmark scores. Table 1 reports each method’s results at the checkpoint with the highest mean accuracy across the three benchmarks.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 shows that BPO achieves 50.5% average accuracy, compared with 39.5% for GRPO-ClipHigher and 47.4% for CISPO, the strongest baseline. These correspond to gains of 11.0 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively. BPO also achieves the highest accuracy on all three benchmarks.

BPO achieves the highest final accuracy (Figure 1). After 400 training steps, its average accuracy is 49.4%, compared with 45.5% for DPPO, the strongest baseline at the end of training.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Bellman Policy Optimization (BPO), a critic-free method for RLVR derived from Policy Mirror Descent. Using the Bellman equations, we obtained a trajectory-level objective that avoids estimating intermediate state values. We proved that this objective and the original PMD objective have the same unique optimal solution on states reachable under the rollout policy. We then derived a practical token-level loss through approximations, with a smoothed mismatch-correction weight replacing the importance-sampling ratio. On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, BPO achieves a peak average accuracy of 50.5%50.5\% across AIME 2024–2026, outperforming GRPO-ClipHigher, GSPO, CISPO, and DPPO by 3.13.1–11.011.0 percentage points. Ablations on Qwen3-4B-Base show similar performance across a range of smoothing and truncation settings.

Appendix A Omitted Proofs

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Sufficiency follows from (24). It remains to prove necessity. We use 𝕀A\mathbb{I}_{A} to denote the indicator of an event AA throughout this section.

Let suppμ(⋅|s)\text{supp}\mu(\cdot|s) denote the set of actions with positive probability under policy μ\mu at state ss. Let suppℙμ(⋅|x)\text{supp}\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x) denote the set of responses with positive probability under policy μ\mu given prompt xx. Let 𝒮xμ\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\mu} denote the set of states reachable from prompt xx with positive probability under policy μ\mu.

Fix any prompt x∈Dx\in D. For any state-action pair (s,a)(s,a), define

dπ(s,a)=ηAμ(s,a)−(logπ(a|s)−logμ(a|s)+DKL(μ(⋅|s)∥π(⋅|s))).\begin{split}d_{\pi}(s,a)=\eta A^{\mu}(s,a)-\Big(\log\pi(a|s)-\log\mu(a|s)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s))\Big).\end{split}

The exponential-form update (17) preserves the support of the rollout policy, so π+∈Πμ\pi^{+}\in\Pi_{\mu} and

Hence, π+\pi^{+} is feasible for (18) and achieves objective value zero. Since the objective is nonnegative, the minimum value of (18) is zero.

Now let π^+∈Πμ\hat{\pi}^{+}\in\Pi_{\mu} be any optimal solution of (18). Since the minimum value is zero and ϕ⁡(x)>0\phi(x)>0, we have

Since π^+,π+∈Πμ\hat{\pi}^{+},\pi^{+}\in\Pi_{\mu}, both policies assign zero probability outside suppμ(⋅|s)\text{supp}\mu(\cdot|s). Therefore,

Thus, c⁡(s)=1c(s)=1, and

π^+(⋅|s)=π+(⋅|s),∀s∈𝒮xμ.\begin{split}\hat{\pi}^{+}(\cdot|s)=\pi^{+}(\cdot|s),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\mu}.\end{split}

In addition, since π^+,π+∈Πμ\hat{\pi}^{+},\pi^{+}\in\Pi_{\mu}, both π+\pi^{+} and π^+\hat{\pi}^{+} assign zero probability outside suppℙμ(⋅|x)\text{supp}\mathbb{P}_{\mu}(\cdot|x). Consequently,

ℙπ^+(⋅|x)=ℙπ+(⋅|x).\begin{split}\mathbb{P}_{\hat{\pi}^{+}}(\cdot|x)=\mathbb{P}_{\pi^{+}}(\cdot|x).\end{split}

A.2 Proof of the Identity (27)

Fix a state ss and an action yy, and let

p=π(y|s),q=μ(y|s).\begin{split}p=\pi(y|s),\quad q=\mu(y|s).\end{split}

The binary KL divergence associated with action yy is

DbinKL(μ(⋅|s)∥π(⋅|s);y)=qlogqp+(1−q)log1−q1−p.\begin{split}D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s);y\right)=q\log\frac{q}{p}+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}.\end{split}

Differentiating with respect to π\pi gives

∇DbinKL(μ(⋅|s)∥π(⋅|s);y)=−q∇logp+1−q1−p∇p.\begin{split}\nabla D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s);y\right)=-q\nabla\log p+\frac{1-q}{1-p}\nabla p.\end{split}

Using the fact that ∇p=p∇logp\nabla p=p\nabla\log p, we obtain

∇(logp+DbinKL(μ(⋅|s)∥π(⋅|s);y))=(1−q)∇logp+(1−q)​p1−p∇logp=1−μ⁡(y|s)1−π⁡(y|s)∇logπ(y|s),\begin{split}\nabla\Big(\log p+D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s);y\right)\Big)=(1-q)\nabla\log p+\frac{(1-q)p}{1-p}\nabla\log p=\frac{1-\mu(y|s)}{1-\pi(y|s)}\nabla\log\pi(y|s),\end{split}

i.e.,

∇(logπ(y|s)+DbinKL(μ(⋅|s)∥π(⋅|s);y))=1−μ⁡(y|s)1−π⁡(y|s)∇logπ(y|s).\begin{split}\nabla\Big(\log\pi(y|s)+D^{\mathrm{bin}}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\mu(\cdot|s)\,\|\,\pi(\cdot|s);y\right)\Big)=\frac{1-\mu(y|s)}{1-\pi(y|s)}\nabla\log\pi(y|s).\end{split}

This proves (27). □\square

Appendix B Experimental Details

All experiments use AdamW with a constant learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98, and weight decay 0.10.1. The gradient clipping threshold is 1.01.0. We use no KL penalty and the entropy bonus coefficient is zero. Training rollouts are sampled at temperature 1.01.0 and top-p=1.0p=1.0, with top-kk filtering disabled. Advantages are centered and normalized by the reward standard deviation within each response group as in GRPO. We use seq-mean-token-mean for loss aggregation. These settings are shared across methods.

We use 400 training steps for the main experiments in Section 4 and 1000 for the ablations in Appendix C. The AIME benchmarks are available on Hugging Face.11 1 AIME24: https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime24, AIME25: https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime25, AIME26: https://huggingface.co/datasets/math-ai/aime26. We evaluate every ten rollout batches (i.e., training steps). All evaluations use 32 responses per question at temperature 1.01.0 and top-p=1.0p=1.0, with top-kk filtering disabled. Evaluation uses the same response-length limit as training for each model.

We report Avg@32 as an estimate of Pass@1. The Avg. column and the plotted average accuracy are the arithmetic mean of the AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26 Avg@32 scores.

We select the checkpoint with the highest mean Avg@32 across the three benchmarks, choosing the earlier step in a tie.

GRPO-ClipHigher uses the asymmetric clipping interval [0.8,1.28][0.8,1.28] from DAPO [4]. CISPO uses an importance-weight cap of 3.03.0, following the configuration used in the stability experiments of DPPO [8]. DPPO uses binary total variation with threshold δ=0.1\delta=0.1, following TMax [35]. GSPO uses the clipping interval [1−3×10−3,1+5×10−3][1-3\times 10^{-3},1+5\times 10^{-3}], following the ablation results in [36]. BPO uses the default setting ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1 and C=3.0C=3.0 in the main experiments.

Appendix C Ablation Studies

We study the two BPO hyperparameters ϵ\epsilon and CC on Qwen3-4B-Base with 1000 training steps. Here, each batch contains 128 prompts with 16 responses per prompt. The 2048 responses are split into four minibatches of 512, with a maximum response length of 8192 tokens. One training step in the figures denotes one rollout batch followed by its minibatch updates. Each sweep changes only one hyperparameter while keeping the other settings fixed. Both sweeps in Section C.1 and Section C.2 use the training setup in Appendix B and share the same GRPO-ClipHigher baseline.

C.1 Sensitivity to ϵ\epsilon

We fix C=3.0C=3.0 and vary ϵ\epsilon over {0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3}\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3\}. Figure 2 shows the training curves, and Table 2 summarizes the results.

BPO achieves similar average accuracies of 25.4%–25.8% for ϵ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2}\epsilon\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}. At ϵ=0.3\epsilon=0.3, accuracy is 24.1%, still 3.6 percentage points above GRPO-ClipHigher. BPO shows little sensitivity to ϵ\epsilon from 0.050.05 to 0.20.2 and outperforms the baseline at all four settings.

C.2 Sensitivity to CC

We fix ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1 and vary CC over {2.0,3.0,4.0}\{2.0,3.0,4.0\}. Figure 3 shows the training curves, and Table 3 summarizes the results.

The three values of CC yield average accuracies between 25.3% and 25.8%, a spread of 0.5 percentage points. All three exceed the GRPO-ClipHigher baseline of 20.5%. These results show that BPO is insensitive to CC from 2.02.0 to 4.04.0.
